Key Concepts

A website needs files, usually HTML, and a server that makes those files available online.
Quarto converts .qmd source files into .html pages.
Saving a source file, rendering a site, committing a snapshot, and pushing to GitHub are separate actions.

Source files are edited by people; output and cache files are generated by tools.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Key Concepts

An object stores a value or a table in R.
A function takes an input, performs an operation, and returns an output.
A tibble is a modern data frame: observations are rows and variables are columns.
dplyr verbs make table operations readable: filter rows, select columns, create variables, sort rows, and summarize groups.
The Decennial Census is a full population count every ten years; the ACS is a continuous sample survey that publishes estimates with margins of error.
A GEOID is a geographic identifier and should be stored as text so leading zeros are preserved.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, you won’t.
In this analysis, I look at the number with a bachelor’s degree across counties in New York State, and ask which communities we measure most and least reliably.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                        estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                          <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Hamilton County, New York        586    99   16.9 
 2 Schuyler County, New York       1570   206   13.1 
 3 Yates County, New York          2427   269   11.1 
 4 Essex County, New York          4885   541   11.1 
 5 Fulton County, New York         5111   541   10.6 
 6 Sullivan County, New York       9476   986   10.4 
 7 Montgomery County, New York     3888   400   10.3 
 8 Washington County, New York     5649   573   10.1

10 Lewis County, New York          2060   203    9.85

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. That means a wide pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                         myvarE myvarM    popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>   <dbl> <dbl>
1 36001 Albany County, New York       49653   1534  315374    NA
2 36003 Allegany County, New York      3787    306   47027    NA
3 36005 Bronx County, New York       130281   3296 1419250    NA
4 36007 Broome County, New York       21526   1008  197738    NA
5 36009 Cattaraugus County, New York   6055    387   76479    NA
6 36011 Cayuga County, New York        7436    457   75464    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 10 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         24        730694.
2 Low confidence           8         40855.
3 Moderate                30         66961.


The 24 high-confidence counties have an average population of approximately 730,694, compared with 66,961 for the 30 moderate-confidence counties and 40,855 for the 8 low-confidence counties. This pattern suggests that more populous counties tend to have more reliable ACS estimates, while smaller counties tend to have larger margins of error relative to their estimates.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
Among all the counties in New York State, Hamilton County has the least reliable estimate: 586 residents aged 25 or older were estimated to have a bachelor’s degree as their highest level of education, with a margin of error of 99, or 16.9% of the estimate. Schuyler County follows with a relative margin of error of 13.1%, while Yates and Essex Counties are both about 11.1%. Overall, eight counties fall into the low-confidence category.
This reflects how the American Community Survey (ACS) works. The ACS estimates population characteristics from a sample rather than counting every resident. Smaller counties contribute fewer sampled households and residents, so each response carries more weight and the estimates have greater uncertainty. In this analysis, low-confidence counties have an average population of 40,855, compared with 730,694 in high-confidence counties.
Ignoring this margin of error might lead to unfair policy decisions. If a state agency directed workforce-development funding toward counties with fewer bachelor’s degree holders, it might treat every county estimate as equally precise. If a small county’s bachelor’s degree count were overestimated, it could appear better educated and receive less support than it needs as the result. Rural counties such as Hamilton, Schuyler, and Yates are especially vulnerable because their limited sample sizes make their estimates less stable. Agencies should consider margins of error and avoid making funding decisions based on small differences alone.

  NAME                      estimate   moe moe_pct
  <chr>                        <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>

This comparison shows that ACS estimates become much less precise at smaller geographic scales because each tract is represented by a smaller sample.

title: Week 2: dplyr and Census
text:
Notes

1. Objects, functions, arguments, and comments
This example keeps counties with populations above 50,000 and stores the result in a new object:
result <- filter(counties, population > 50000) # Keep larger counties

result is the object that stores the output.
<- is the assignment operator.
filter() is the function.
counties is the input data.
population > 50000 is an argument or condition.
Text after # is a comment and is not executed.

R is case-sensitive, so result and Result are different objects. Using lowercase object and function names consistently prevents avoidable errors.


2. Packages: install once, load each session
A package is a collection of functions. Installation happens once on a computer; loading happens at the start of each new R session.
# Run once on a computer
install.packages("dplyr")
install.packages("tidycensus")

# Run in each new R session
library(dplyr)
library(tidycensus)
I think of install.packages() as putting a book on the shelf and library() as taking that book off the shelf to use it.


3. Tibbles and dplyr verbs
A tibble is a table in which each row is an observation and each column is a variable.



NAME
INCOME
MOE




Adams
78,975
1,237


Berks
74,617
4,372


Bucks
104,200
2,374



Common dplyr verbs:

filter() keeps rows that meet a condition.
select() keeps or reorders columns.
mutate() adds or changes a computed column.
arrange() changes row order; desc() requests descending order.
group_by() and summarize() turn many rows into group-level summaries.

A correct mutate() expression must name the new column:
counties <- counties |>
  mutate(income_doubled = income * 2)
The same sequence of operations can be written step by step:
step_1 <- filter(counties, moe_pct > 10)
step_2 <- arrange(step_1, desc(moe_pct))
step_3 <- select(step_2, NAME, moe_pct)
Or as one pipeline. Both %>% and the base-R pipe |> mean roughly “and then.”
new_data <- counties |>
  filter(moe_pct > 10) |>
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) |>
  select(NAME, moe_pct)
Grouping allows us to calculate one value for each category:
county_income |>
  group_by(STATE) |>
  summarize(min_income = min(INCOME))


4. Decennial Census and the ACS
The two Census Bureau products answer different questions:








Product
What it provides
Important limitation




Decennial Census
A full population count every 10 years, down to Census blocks
Limited social and economic characteristics


American Community Survey
Ongoing sample-based estimates for income, education, housing, commuting, and more
Every estimate includes uncertainty



Important ACS products:

ACS 1-year: more current, but available only for areas with populations of 65,000 or more.
ACS 5-year: combines five years of responses, covers small geographies, and is generally more precise for tract or block-group analysis.
ACS 3-year: discontinued after the 2013 release.

For ACS data, always keep two values in mind:
Estimate (E)        the estimated value
Margin of Error (M) the uncertainty around that estimate


5. Census geography and GEOIDs
The basic geographic hierarchy is:
state -> county -> Census tract -> block group -> Census block
Census tract boundaries can change over time. Block groups are available in ACS 5-year data, but their smaller samples often produce large margins of error, so they should be used cautiously rather than rejected automatically. Census blocks are primarily associated with Decennial Census data.
A tract GEOID has 11 digits. For example:
42101000100
42     = Pennsylvania state FIPS
101    = Philadelphia County FIPS
000100 = Census tract code
GEOIDs are identifiers, not quantities, so they should be stored as character strings:
geoid <- "42101000100"


6. ACS variable codes and tidycensus
In the raw ACS name B19013_001E:

B19013 is the table number.
001 is the line number.
E means estimate; M means margin of error.

When using tidycensus, the variable is normally requested without the final E or M:
library(tidycensus)

county_data <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(
    median_income = "B19013_001",
    total_population = "B01003_001"
  ),
  state = "PA",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)


7. Long and wide data

Long (tidy) output: one geography-variable combination per row, with variable, estimate, and moe columns.
Wide output: one geographic unit per row, with separate estimate and MOE columns such as median_incomeE and median_incomeM.

Long format is useful for repeated operations across variables; wide format is often convenient for comparison, modeling, and joins.

title: Week 1: Getting Set Up
text:
Notes

1. What is a website?
In the class workflow, a website has two main parts:
a folder of HTML files + a server that is always online
For this portfolio:
Quarto creates the HTML files
GitHub Pages hosts those files online
The complete path from source to website is:
.qmd source file -> Quarto Render -> .html page -> GitHub Pages
I normally edit the .qmd source rather than the generated .html file.


2. Quarto and Render
Quarto is a publishing system that combines writing, code, and results in one document. It can render a .qmd file as a webpage, PDF, slide deck, or Word document.
When I select Render, Quarto:

Reads the .qmd file from top to bottom.
Finds executable code chunks.
Sends R code to R and receives the results.
Combines the writing, code, and output into HTML.

Saving only records edits in the source file. Rendering rebuilds the output page, so Save is not Render.


3. Anatomy of a .qmd file
A Quarto document normally contains three parts:
YAML header + Markdown text + R code chunks

YAML header
The YAML header goes at the very top and stores page metadata:
---
title: "Week 1: Getting Set Up"
description: "My first weekly note"
date: 2026-08-28
---
Important YAML rules:

The opening and closing --- lines matter.
A colon must be followed by a space.
Dates should use YYYY-MM-DD.
Use plain quotation marks.



Markdown
Markdown provides headings, paragraphs, lists, emphasis, and links:
## What I Learned

This is a paragraph with a [link](https://quarto.org/).

- First point
- Second point


R code chunks
An executable R chunk in a Quarto file uses an opening fence labeled {r}. The code inside a chunk might look like this:
library(tidycensus)

x <- 2 + 2
print(x)
R code should be placed inside a code chunk when I want Quarto to run it and include the result in the page.



4. Files and folders
A useful question is: Who is this file for?
Files I edit directly:
index.qmd
about.qmd
weekly-notes/*.qmd
assignments/*.qmd
_quarto.yml
Files and folders mainly used by software:







Item
Purpose




.Rproj
Opens the folder as an RStudio project


.gitignore
Tells Git which files not to track


.Renviron
Stores environment variables and secrets such as API keys


docs/
Contains the rendered website published by GitHub Pages


_freeze/
Stores Quarto execution results and cache data



The key rule is: edit source files and allow Quarto to regenerate output files.


5. Why index.qmd matters
Web servers normally look for index.html when a visitor requests a folder URL. Quarto creates that file from index.qmd:
index.qmd -> Render -> docs/index.html
That is why the portfolio homepage source file is named index.qmd.


6. Git, GitHub.com, and GitHub Desktop
These tools are related but have different roles:

Git is the version-control system running locally on my computer.
GitHub.com stores an online copy of the repository.
GitHub Desktop provides buttons and menus that send commands to Git.

Commit and push are also different:
Commit = save a labeled snapshot in the local Git repository
Push   = send local commits to GitHub.com


7. The portfolio workflow
Edit -> Save -> Render -> Commit -> Push -> wait -> refresh the live site
Each step changes a different version of the work:

Edit and Save: update the local source file.
Render: rebuild the local website output.
Commit: record a labeled local snapshot.
Push: transfer commits to GitHub.com.
Refresh: check the published GitHub Pages site.



8. Markdown, R scripts, and Quarto documents
Markdown text = writing and formatting, without calculation
R script      = reusable code
.qmd document = writing + code + results
An R script is useful for experimenting with code and building reusable analysis. A .qmd document is useful when I need to explain the analysis and publish its results together.

title: Assignment 3：Verify the Claim of Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 2: Test

Poverty rates and margins of error
Because the poverty rate is a proportion, I calculate its 90% margin of error with moe_prop().


Show code
poverty_2010 <- poverty_2010 %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate = below_povertyE / totalE,
    poverty_rate_moe = moe_prop(
      num = below_povertyE,
      denom = totalE,
      moe_num = below_povertyM,
      moe_denom = totalM
    )
  )

poverty_2017 <- poverty_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate = below_povertyE / totalE,
    poverty_rate_moe = moe_prop(
      num = below_povertyE,
      denom = totalE,
      moe_num = below_povertyM,
      moe_denom = totalM
    )
  )




Missing values
First I check 2006–2010 for zero denominators or missing estimates.


Show code
missing_2010 <- poverty_2010 %>%
  filter(
    totalE == 0 |
      is.na(poverty_rate) |
      is.na(poverty_rate_moe)
  )

dim(missing_2010)


[1] 7 8


dim() reports rows, then columns. The seven rows are tracts with no valid 2006–2010 rate.
The same check for 2013–2017 gives:


Show code
missing_2017 <- poverty_2017 %>%
  filter(
    totalE == 0 |
      is.na(poverty_rate) |
      is.na(poverty_rate_moe)
  )

dim(missing_2017)


[1] 8 8


Eight tracts have no valid 2013–2017 rate. In both periods, invalid rates come from zero denominators, so I exclude them rather than treat them as zero. Matching leaves 376 usable tracts.


Reliability
I calculate CV as (MOE / 1.645) / poverty rate * 100. Following Jurjevich et al. (2018), CV below 12% is High confidence, 12–40% is Moderate, and above 40% is Low confidence.


Show code
poverty_2010_valid <- poverty_2010 %>%
  filter(
    totalE > 0,
    !is.na(poverty_rate),
    !is.na(poverty_rate_moe)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    period = "2006–2010",
    poverty_rate_se = poverty_rate_moe / 1.645,
    cv = poverty_rate_se / poverty_rate * 100,
    reliability = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "High confidence",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Moderate",
      TRUE     ~ "Low confidence"
    )
  )

poverty_2017_valid <- poverty_2017 %>%
  filter(
    totalE > 0,
    !is.na(poverty_rate),
    !is.na(poverty_rate_moe)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    period = "2013–2017",
    poverty_rate_se = poverty_rate_moe / 1.645,
    cv = poverty_rate_se / poverty_rate * 100,
    reliability = case_when(
      cv < 12  ~ "High confidence",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Moderate",
      TRUE     ~ "Low confidence"
    )
  )

city_rate_2017 <- sum(poverty_2017_valid$below_povertyE) /
  sum(poverty_2017_valid$totalE)



Reliability in 2006–2010

poverty_2010_valid %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_tracts = n()
  ) %>%

Most estimates are Moderate: 321 in 2006–2010 and 332 in 2013–2017. High-confidence counts are 11 and 22; low-confidence counts are 45 and 22.



Change between periods


Show code
poverty_wide <- bind_rows(
  poverty_2010_valid,
  poverty_2017_valid
) %>%
  select(GEOID, NAME, period, poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe) %>%
  pivot_wider(
    names_from = period,
    values_from = c(poverty_rate, poverty_rate_moe)
  )

poverty_tested <- poverty_wide %>%
  filter(
    !is.na(`poverty_rate_2006–2010`),
    !is.na(`poverty_rate_2013–2017`)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    change = `poverty_rate_2013–2017` - `poverty_rate_2006–2010`,
    se_1 = `poverty_rate_moe_2006–2010` / 1.645,
    se_2 = `poverty_rate_moe_2013–2017` / 1.645,
    se_diff = sqrt(se_1^2 + se_2^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645,
    result = case_when(
      significant & change > 0 ~ "Significant increase",
      significant & change < 0 ~ "Significant decrease",
      TRUE ~ "Not statistically detectable"
    )
  )

change_counts <- poverty_tested %>%
  count(result)




Show code
ggplot(change_counts, aes(x = result, y = n)) +
  geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Results of the tract-level change test",
    subtitle = "Individual 90% tests for 376 matched Philadelphia census tracts",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Number of tracts",
    caption = "Source: U.S. Census Bureau, ACS five-year estimates."
  )





Most Philadelphia tracts did not have a statistically detectable change in poverty rate.






Error-bar visualization
The figure shows the 20 largest detectable changes; the counts above include all 376 tracts.


Show code
change_plot_data <- poverty_tested %>%
  filter(significant) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(change))) %>%
  slice_head(n = 20) %>%
  mutate(
    NAME = str_remove(NAME, ", Philadelphia County, Pennsylvania"),
    change_pp = change * 100,
    moe_diff_pp = moe_diff * 100,
    direction = case_when(
      change > 0 ~ "Increase",
      TRUE ~ "Decrease"
    )
  )

change_plot_data %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, change_pp), y = change_pp)) +
  geom_col(aes(fill = direction)) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = change_pp - moe_diff_pp,
                    ymax = change_pp + moe_diff_pp), width = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed") +
  coord_flip() +
  theme_minimal() +
  labs(
    title = "Largest statistically detectable changes in poverty rate",
    subtitle = "Twenty largest absolute tract changes, 2006–2010 vs. 2013–2017",
    x = NULL,
    y = "Change in poverty rate (percentage points)",
    fill = NULL,
    caption = "Error bars show 90% margins of error; dashed line marks no change. Source: U.S. Census Bureau ACS."
  )





Largest statistically detectable tract-level changes in poverty rates, with 90% margins of error.




At 90% confidence, 63 of 376 tracts changed detectably: 36 increased and 27 decreased; 313 showed no detectable change. Poverty change was therefore uneven.

text:
Part 3: Adjudicate
Supported. Combining the tract counts gives a 2013–2017 city poverty rate of 25.8%, consistent with the article’s 26% figure. Poverty also increased in some places: 36 of 376 tracts show detectable increases. Not supported as a tract-level generalization. The increase was not widespread: 313 tracts show no detectable change and 27 show decreases.
Cannot be determined. The Fairhill, Eastwick, and Holmesburg figures cannot be reproduced because the article does not provide its tract-to-neighborhood crosswalk; the Holmesburg claim also requires race-specific data. Explanations involving opioids, migration, or displacement are beyond what these ACS estimates can establish.

title: Assignment 3：Verify the Claim of Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 4: Rewrite

Philadelphia’s poverty rate was about 25.8% in the 2013–2017 ACS. Change within the city was uneven: of 376 comparable census tracts, 36 had detectable increases, 27 had detectable decreases, and 313 had no detectable change at 90% confidence. Poverty worsened in some places, but not as a widespread tract-level pattern. The reported Fairhill, Eastwick, and Holmesburg figures cannot be reproduced because the article did not publish its tract-to-neighborhood crosswalk. The Holmesburg claim also requires race-specific poverty data.

section: Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
text:
Part 5: Buffers, filters, and cutting the dough
Build a half-mile zone around every station and merge the circles into one shape. Remember your units.

station_zone <- stations %>%
  st_buffer(dist = 0.5*5280) %>%
  st_union()

Pick whole cookies: which tracts don’t touch the zone at all?

outside_zone <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_filter(station_zone, .predicate = st_disjoint)

nrow(outside_zone)

[1] 162


Cut the dough: what share of each tract’s area falls inside the zone?

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  mutate(tract_area = as.numeric(st_area(.)))

covered <- philly_tracts %>%
  st_intersection(station_zone) %>%
  mutate(covered_area = as.numeric(st_area(.))) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(GEOID, covered_area)

philly_tracts <- philly_tracts %>%
  left_join(covered, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(pct_covered = replace_na(covered_area / tract_area, 0) * 100)

Notice: that last step is the left_join() from Part 1b. It’s a join by what (GEOID), used to bring a join-by-where result back into the table. The two kinds of join work together.

Part 2: Look before you model
The Week 3 habit comes first: plot the relationship before you fit anything.

ggplot(tracts, aes(x = med_incE, y = med_rentE)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "red") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::dollar) +

       title = "Rent and income, Philadelphia tracts") +

Stop and look: Does a straight line describe this cloud well everywhere, or does it bend? Where are the points that sit far from the line?
The relationship is strongly positive but not perfectly linear: it starts to flatten among the highest-income tracts. A few low- and middle-income tracts have rents far above the line, and one very high-income tract has rent far below it.

Look at the n_stations coefficient. Answer both questions in one or two sentences each:

β̂ reading: Can you tell the housing agency that bike share stations raise rents? Why or why not?
Your answer: No. Holding the included variables constant, one additional nearby station is associated with about $5.48 higher monthly rent, but this observational coefficient does not establish causation. Stations may be placed in already-expensive, amenity-rich areas, and omitted neighborhood characteristics or reverse causality can explain the association.

text:
Part 5: Uncertainty in input data
Our Y is an ACS estimate with its own margin of error. Add the residuals to the table and check whether the biggest misses happen where the estimate is least reliable.

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(fitted_m2 = fitted(m2),
         resid_m2  = residuals(m2))

ggplot(tracts, aes(x = rent_cv, y = abs(resid_m2))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_smooth(se = FALSE) +
  labs(x = "CV of the median rent estimate (%)",
       y = "Size of the model's miss ($)",
       title = "Are the biggest misses in the noisiest tracts?") +
  theme_minimal()








Stop and look: If a tract’s rent estimate has a CV of 35%, how much of the model’s miss there could be survey noise rather than a model failure? What does that mean for flagging “tracts with rents above expectation”?
A 35% rent CV means the standard error is 35% of the estimate, so the ACS 90% margin of error is about \(1.645 \times 35\% = 57.6\%\) of the reported rent. A large share—and potentially all—of an apparent residual could therefore be sampling noise. The agency should attach reliability information to every flag and verify high-CV tracts before acting.

title: Week 5 In-Class Lab: Where the Model Is Wrong
text:
Part 6: Fit vs. prediction






WarningTwo different CVs



Week 3 CV = coefficient of variation: how noisy is one estimate? Today’s CV = cross-validation: how well does a model predict data it hasn’t seen? Same letters, unrelated ideas.



6A: One train/test split

set.seed(5080)
n <- nrow(tracts)
train_idx <- sample(1:n, size = 0.8 * n)

train_data <- tracts[train_idx, ]
test_data  <- tracts[-train_idx, ]

m2_train <- lm(med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations,
               data = train_data)

test_pred <- predict(m2_train, newdata = test_data)

rmse_train <- sqrt(mean(residuals(m2_train)^2))
rmse_test  <- sqrt(mean((test_data$med_rentE - test_pred)^2))

c(train = rmse_train, test = rmse_test)

   train     test 
252.6854 265.7514 


Stop and look: Which RMSE is larger? Why would you expect that? In words: “The model’s typical miss on tracts it hasn’t seen is about $266 per month.”
The test RMSE ($265.75) is larger than the training RMSE ($252.69), as expected because the model was optimized on the training observations. The model’s typical miss on tracts it has not seen is about $266 per month for this split.
Change the seed to any other number and rerun the chunk. Did the test RMSE change? That’s why one split isn’t enough.


6B: 10-fold cross-validation
caret wants a plain data frame, so drop the geometry first. (The geometry isn’t a predictor, and train() will choke on it.)

model_df <- tracts %>% st_drop_geometry()

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

set.seed(5080)
cv_m1 <- train(med_rentE ~ med_incE,
               data = model_df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)

set.seed(5080)
cv_m2 <- train(med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations,
               data = model_df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)

text:
Part 7: Where is the model wrong?

7A: Residuals vs. fitted

ggplot(tracts, aes(x = fitted_m2, y = resid_m2)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red") +
  labs(x = "Predicted rent", y = "Residual (actual − predicted)") +
  theme_minimal()







bptest(m2)


    studentized Breusch-Pagan test

data:  m2
BP = 13.807, df = 4, p-value = 0.007938


Stop and look: Random cloud, funnel, or curve? If it’s a funnel, the predictions aren’t biased, but one RMSE hides the fact that the model misses by much more in some tracts. Which tracts?
The plot is closer to a funnel than a random cloud: residual spread grows at higher fitted rents. The Breusch–Pagan test also rejects constant variance (\(p \approx 0.008\)). The model therefore misses by more in the higher-rent, higher-predicted-rent tracts.


7B: The map
The residuals are already a column in an sf data frame. Mapping them is one geom_sf() away.

ggplot(tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = resid_m2), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "grey95", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0, labels = scales::dollar) +
  theme_void() +
  labs(title = "Where the rent model is wrong",
       subtitle = "Red = rent higher than predicted · Blue = lower than predicted",
       fill = "Residual")








Stop and look: If the errors were random, the map would look speckled. Does it? Where do the reds sit together? What might those places have in common that the model doesn’t know about?
Write down your answer. We’ll come back to it in Weeks 6 and 7.
The residuals are spatially clustered rather than speckled. Nearby red and blue tracts form patches around central and university-adjacent areas and in parts of North and Northeast Philadelphia. This suggests that the model is missing place-based factors such as access to jobs and transit, universities, neighborhood amenities, and housing type.

title: Week 5 In-Class Lab: Where the Model Is Wrong
text:
Part 8: The Challenge
Your team’s job: build the best model for predicting tract median rent, then use it to answer the agency’s question.

Rules

The grade is 10-fold CV RMSE. Use model_df (or tracts) and run set.seed(5080) directly before train(), exactly as in Part 6B, so every team is tested on the same folds.
Don’t drop rows. If you add a variable with missing values, you change the folds and the comparison stops being fair. Fill the gaps or choose a different variable.
You may add any ACS variables (use load_variables(2023, "acs5") to browse) and any spatial feature you can build with Week 4 tools: distances, buffers, counts.
You may not use anything built from rent itself. That rules out med_rentM, rent_cv, rent burden (B25071), and the rent distribution tables (B25063). Ask yourself: would the agency have this variable for a tract whose rent it’s trying to predict? If not, using it is cheating the test. That’s called leakage.



Deliver

Your CV RMSE, in dollars, written as a sentence.
One feature you added, and why. What did you think it would capture that the census variables miss? Did it help?
One coefficient, read twice. Pick a variable in your final model and give its β̂ reading and its ŷ reading in one sentence each.
The agency’s list. Using your final model fit to all tracts, find the five tracts with the largest positive residuals (rent well above expectation). For each, report the residual and the rent CV. Which of the five would you tell the agency to trust, and which might be fog?
Your residual map. Did your added features make the clusters from Part 7B shrink?


# Pull only non-rent predictors. None is calculated from median rent.

  geography = "tract",
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2023,
  output = "wide",
  variables = c(
    med_home_value   = "B25077_001",
    med_age          = "B01002_001",
    housing_units    = "B25001_001",
    vacant_units     = "B25002_003",
    poverty_total    = "B17001_001",
    poverty_below    = "B17001_002",
    hh_total         = "B08201_001",
    no_vehicle       = "B08201_002",
    med_year_built   = "B25035_001",
    commute_total    = "B08301_001",
    transit          = "B08301_010",
    walk             = "B08301_019",
    work_from_home   = "B08301_021",
    structure_total  = "B25024_001",
    units_20_49      = "B25024_008",
    units_50_plus    = "B25024_009",
    avg_hh_size      = "B25010_001"
  )
)

# Coordinates let the model learn a smooth two-dimensional location surface.
center_xy <- tracts %>%
  st_centroid() %>%
  st_coordinates()

challenge_df <- tracts %>%
  left_join(challenge_acs, by = "GEOID") %>%
  mutate(
    pct_vacant = vacant_unitsE / housing_unitsE * 100,
    pct_poverty = poverty_belowE / poverty_totalE * 100,
    pct_no_vehicle = no_vehicleE / hh_totalE * 100,
    pct_transit = transitE / commute_totalE * 100,
    pct_walk = walkE / commute_totalE * 100,
    pct_wfh = work_from_homeE / commute_totalE * 100,
    pct_large_building = (units_20_49E + units_50_plusE) /
      structure_totalE * 100,
    x_coord = as.numeric(scale(center_xy[, "X"])),
    y_coord = as.numeric(scale(center_xy[, "Y"]))
  ) %>%
  st_drop_geometry()

# Median-impute only the added X variables, preserving all 377 original rows.
challenge_vars <- c(
  "med_home_valueE", "med_ageE", "pct_vacant", "pct_poverty",
  "pct_no_vehicle", "med_year_builtE", "pct_transit", "pct_walk",
  "pct_wfh", "pct_large_building", "avg_hh_sizeE"
)

for (v in challenge_vars) {
  good <- is.finite(challenge_df[[v]])
  challenge_df[[v]][!good] <- median(challenge_df[[v]][good])
}

baseline_formula <- med_rentE ~
  med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations +
  poly(log(med_home_valueE), 2, raw = TRUE) +
  pct_vacant + pct_poverty + pct_no_vehicle +
  med_ageE + med_year_builtE +
  poly(x_coord, 2, raw = TRUE) * poly(y_coord, 2, raw = TRUE)

  baseline_formula,
  . ~ . + pct_large_building
)

final_formula <- update(
  building_formula,
  . ~ . +
  pct_transit + pct_walk + pct_wfh + avg_hh_sizeE
)

stopifnot(nrow(challenge_df) == nrow(model_df))

  baseline_formula, data = challenge_df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl
)

set.seed(5080)

  building_formula, data = challenge_df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl
)

  final_formula,
  data = challenge_df,
  method = "lm",

1. CV RMSE. The final model’s 10-fold CV RMSE is $218.22, meaning its typical out-of-fold prediction error is about $218 per month. This is about $34.74 lower than m2.
2. Added feature. I added pct_large_building, the share of housing units in buildings with at least 20 units. It captures housing form and dense apartment markets that the demographic predictors miss. Adding it to the otherwise comparable challenge model lowered CV RMSE from about $229.05 to $222.53; the full feature set lowered it further to $218.22.
3. One coefficient, read twice.

β̂ reading: Holding the other model terms constant, a one-percentage-point increase in the share of units in large buildings is associated with about $4.35 higher tract median monthly rent. Because the data are observational, this is not a causal effect of constructing large buildings.
ŷ reading: For prediction, that same coefficient adds about $4.35 to expected monthly rent for each additional percentage point of large-building units, and the feature stays because it improves out-of-sample RMSE.

4. The agency’s list. The table reports the five largest positive residuals. I would place the most trust in tracts 369.02, 314.01, and 220, whose rent CVs are 6.7%, 1.9%, and 5.1%. Tract 117 is moderately reliable (13.5% CV), but its $1,173 residual is so large that it still deserves review. Tract 332 is the clearest fog case: its 28.0% CV implies substantial ACS sampling uncertainty, so the agency should verify it before acting.
5. Residual map. The broad clusters shrink and the CV RMSE falls substantially after adding housing, commute, and smooth location features, but the map is not pure noise. A few isolated deep-red tracts remain, so unmeasured local amenities and ACS uncertainty still matter.

Before you present, discuss

One of your variables is not statistically significant, but removing it makes CV RMSE worse. Do you keep it? What would your Spatial Statistics instructor say, and why is neither of you wrong?
A council member sees your model and says, “So your model proves that renters drive up rents.” What do you say?
If the agency uses your top-five list to target inspections, whose rents does a model error hurt most?

Discussion answers:

I would keep a statistically insignificant variable if repeated cross-validation shows that it reduces RMSE. The prediction task rewards out-of-sample accuracy; a Spatial Statistics course focused on inference may instead remove it because its conditional effect is too uncertain. Those are different goals, so neither decision is inconsistent.
The model does not prove that renters drive up rents. pct_renter is an observational predictor entangled with housing type, location, and selection; its coefficient is conditional association, not a causal effect.
False positives can direct scrutiny and resources toward residents and landlords in the wrong places, while false negatives can hide genuinely excessive rents. The harm is greatest for low-income renters and residents of high-CV tracts, whose noisy estimates make them easier to misclassify.

title: Assignment 4: Building Features, Watching What Happens
text:
Part 7: Reflection
Robbery density was the most useful open-data feature. Adding it to the ACS baseline reduced CV RMSE from 12.33 to 10.86 percentage points, a 1.47-point improvement. Normalizing by area helps separate incident concentration from tract size. Distance to City Hall then absorbed part of the central-versus-peripheral pattern, and its squared term improved the linear-distance model from 9.62 to 9.34. These features may capture overlapping aspects of density, accessibility, and neighborhood conditions; their performance does not identify a causal mechanism.
The sidewalk features disappointed me. Their initial gains were small, and removing both from the quadratic model gave a slightly lower RMSE of 9.32. Complaints depend on reporting and may add little beyond centrality. Logging robbery density also worsened prediction, despite making the histogram less skewed.
β̂ reading: Holding the other final-model terms constant, a one-percentage-point higher renter share is associated with about 0.18 percentage points more households without a vehicle. ŷ reading: If two tracts have identical values for the other predictors, increasing renter share by ten percentage points raises the model’s predicted no-vehicle share by about 1.82 points.
The final map still underpredicts some North and West Philadelphia tracts. I would next measure transit service frequency and walking access using historical 2023 SEPTA GTFS schedules, checking archive coverage before using them. Distance to City Hall cannot represent route quality, transfers, or physical barriers.
Finally, the uncertainty plot does not show a simple increase in error with CV: several large misses have reasonably reliable ACS estimates. A median outcome standard error of 5.50 points indicates meaningful noise, but it cannot be subtracted from RMSE to isolate model error. Sampling uncertainty, omitted variables, and imperfect functional form all remain plausible. The 24.4% improvement is encouraging, but reused random folds and a few negative predictions limit immediate policy use.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Model Evaluation
text:
Key Concepts

Prediction asks for an accurate \(\hat y\); coefficient inference asks what we can learn about \(\beta\). Neither automatically establishes causation.
A residual is observed minus fitted: \(e_i=y_i-\hat y_i\). Positive means rent is higher than predicted; negative means lower.
Ordinary least squares minimizes squared vertical residuals.
A good training fit does not guarantee accurate predictions on new tracts.
Evaluate candidate models using the same rows, folds, outcome units, and metric.
Survey coefficient of variation and model cross-validation both abbreviate to CV, but answer different questions.

title: Week 5: Regression, Prediction, and Model Evaluation
text:
Notes

1. The modeling table and the question
Each row represents a tract, not a household. The target is a tract-level median monthly gross rent. Income is a tract-level median annual household income.








Variable
Role and meaning
Unit or check




GEOID
Tract identifier
Character text; preserve leading zeros


med_rentE
Outcome: estimated median gross rent
Dollars per month


med_incE
Predictor: estimated median household income
Dollars per year


pct_renter
Renter-occupied / all occupied housing units
Lab uses 0–100, not 0–1


pct_ba
BA or higher / population age 25+
Lab uses 0–100


n_stations
Number of nearby Indego bike-share stations
Count, not a causal treatment


rent_cv
Relative sampling uncertainty of the rent estimate
Percent


geometry
Tract polygon
Keep for spatial calculations and mapping



The handwritten 0.71 corresponds to a proportion of 71%; the lab’s percentage variable would be 71. With a 0–100 predictor, increasing it by 1 means one percentage point. With a 0–1 proportion, one percentage point is 0.01. The renter denominator is occupied housing units, not all residents.
The lab counts stations within half a mile of the tract polygon. A station inside a tract has distance zero; one near any part of its boundary may count. This does not establish that every resident is within a half-mile walk.
tracts <- philly_tracts |>
  mutate(
    pct_renter = 100 * renter_occE / occ_unitsE,
    pct_ba = 100 * (baE + maE + profE + phdE) / edu_totalE,
    rent_se = med_rentM / 1.645,
    rent_cv = 100 * rent_se / med_rentE
  )
Before fitting, check positive denominators and finite values. Build a common analysis sample for all candidate models, report which rows were lost, and keep GEOIDs in the same order. Otherwise lm() may omit rows and residuals may no longer line up with the map.


2. The unknown relationship, fitted values, and errors
The conceptual data-generating relationship is
\[
Y=f(X)+\epsilon.
\]
Here \(f\) is an unknown relationship, \(X\) is the available information, and \(\epsilon\) is remaining variation. A simple linear model approximates it by
\[
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_i+\epsilon_i,
\qquad \hat Y_i=\hat\beta_0+\hat\beta_1X_i.
\]
The prediction formula has no added unknown \(\epsilon_i\): we cannot know that individual error in advance. The theoretical error \(\epsilon_i\) and fitted residual \(e_i\) are related but distinct; residuals become observable after fitting.








Objective
Example question
Evidence to examine




Prediction, \(\hat y\)
What monthly rent should we expect for a tract?
Held-out errors and stability


Inference, \(\hat\beta\)
How much does predicted rent differ with income, conditional on included predictors?
Coefficients, uncertainty, assumptions


Causal inference
Would installing a station change rent?
A credible causal design, beyond an observational coefficient



An Indego-station count can help prediction by representing centrality or amenities. That predictive usefulness does not prove that stations cause rents to increase. Tract relationships also do not establish individual household relationships: that would risk an ecological inference error.


3. Flexibility and model families
The board placed linear models at the simpler end and trees, forests, boosting, and neural networks toward the more flexible end. Treat this as an intuition, not a universal ranking. Flexibility depends on features and tuning: a shallow tree may be simple, while a linear regression with many basis functions may be flexible.

Linear regression specifies a form and estimates its coefficients.
Ridge and lasso regularize coefficients; with the same features, their penalties generally constrain flexibility rather than automatically increasing it.
Logistic regression models probabilities for a categorical outcome. It is not simply the next more flexible model for predicting a continuous rent amount.
Nonparametric methods allow the fitted relationship’s complexity to adapt more to the data. “Nonparametric” does not mean that there are no parameters or assumptions.

Greater flexibility can reduce underfitting but may fit accidental patterns in the training sample. Validation tells us whether the extra complexity helps.


4. How least squares chooses the line
For every observation, compute a residual and square it:
\[
e_i=y_i-\hat y_i,
\qquad RSS=\sum_i e_i^2.
\]
OLS chooses coefficients that minimize \(RSS\). Squaring stops positive and negative residuals from canceling and gives larger misses greater weight. The distances are vertical, in the outcome direction; OLS does not minimize the shortest perpendicular distance to the line.



Simulated residuals and variance patterns. Vertical segments show observed minus fitted rent; the two residual plots contrast constant and increasing spread.




5. Reading lm() output in meaningful units
m1 <- lm(med_rentE ~ med_incE, data = tracts)
summary(m1)
coef(m1)["med_incE"] * 10000
The rounded board example gives this fitted equation:
\[
\widehat{\text{monthly rent}}=690+0.0081\times\text{annual income}.
\]
An income difference of $10,000 corresponds to an $81 difference in predicted monthly rent. At income $82,000, predicted rent is $1,354.20. If observed rent is $1,650, the residual is $295.80: observed rent exceeds the prediction.
The intercept is the prediction at income zero. This can be outside the data’s useful range, so it is not necessarily a meaningful description of actual tracts.







Output
Interpretation




Estimate
Fitted coefficient, with units determined by \(Y\) and \(X\)


Standard error
Estimated uncertainty of the coefficient, not a tract’s prediction error


t statistic
(estimate - null value) / SE; the usual null value is zero


p-value
Under the null and assumptions, probability of a statistic at least this extreme



For the board slope and rounded SE, \(0.0081/0.0005=16.2\). A two-sided 5% test uses a t critical value based on residual degrees of freedom; 1.96 is a large- sample approximation. A small p-value does not measure predictive accuracy, practical importance, or the probability that the null hypothesis is true.
In multiple regression, a slope describes an association holding the other included predictors constant. Changing the model can change that slope.


6. Noise in the outcome and in predictors
Random outcome measurement error that is mean-zero conditional on the predictors adds uncertainty and tends to enlarge residuals; it does not by itself create a systematic slope bias. Outcome errors related to predictors can bias results. Residuals may also contain omitted systematic patterns, model misspecification, and spatial dependence, not just random noise.
Classical independent measurement error in the single predictor of a simple regression tends to shrink its slope toward zero: attenuation bias. In multiple regression or with nonclassical measurement error, the direction is not guaranteed. The board’s “noise in X flattens the slope” needs these conditions.
ACS median rent is itself an estimate. Its 90% margin of error can be converted approximately to a standard error by dividing by 1.645. For a positive estimate,
\[
CV_{\text{estimate}}=100\times\frac{SE}{\text{estimate}}.
\]
A 35% CV means the SE is 35% of the estimate; the 90% MOE is approximately 57.6% of it. It does not tell us exactly what fraction of a model residual is sampling noise. Large residuals should be considered alongside estimate uncertainty before being treated as policy flags.


7. Training fit versus prediction performance
For an ordinary unweighted model with an intercept, training
\[
R^2=1-\frac{\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2}{\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2}.
\]
Adding predictors on the same training rows cannot decrease ordinary training \(R^2\), even if the additions do not generalize. Adjusted \(R^2\) penalizes complexity but still does not replace held-out evaluation. \(R^2\) can also be calculated out of sample, where it can be negative; always state which data produced a metric.
RMSE takes the root of the average squared prediction error:
\[
RMSE=\sqrt{\frac{1}{n}\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2}.
\]
For observed rents (500, 900) and predictions (400, 1200), the errors are (100, -300), squared errors are (10000, 90000), and RMSE is about $223.61. RMSE has the same units as rent and emphasizes large errors. It is not the mean absolute error (which is $200 in this example).
summary(lm)$sigma uses residual degrees of freedom in its denominator, whereas training RMSE uses \(n\). They need not match.


8. Train/test splits and K-fold cross-validation
An 80/20 split fits a model on 80% of observations and evaluates predictions on the unused 20%. Training error is usually smaller, though an individual random split can be an exception. A single split can give a lucky or unlucky result.
Five-fold CV partitions 100 records into five groups of 20. Fit five separate models, each on 80 records, and predict the remaining 20. Every observation gets one out-of-fold prediction from a model that did not train on that observation.



Five-fold cross-validation: the validation fold rotates while the other four folds train the model.


Two legitimate summaries are often both called “CV RMSE”:
\[
\text{mean fold RMSE}=\frac{1}{K}\sum_k RMSE_k,
\]
\[
\text{pooled OOF RMSE}=\sqrt{\frac{\sum_k n_k RMSE_k^2}{\sum_k n_k}}.
\]
They generally differ because taking a square root and taking an average do not commute. The Week 6 helper uses pooled out-of-fold RMSE; the lab’s caret output typically reports the mean resampled RMSE. Use one definition consistently.
The following base-R pattern makes the common folds explicit. It assumes a previously prepared complete model_df, with one row per tract.
model_df <- sf::st_drop_geometry(tracts)
set.seed(5080)
fold_id <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out = nrow(model_df)))
oof <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(model_df))

for (k in sort(unique(fold_id))) {
  holdout <- fold_id == k
  fit <- lm(med_rentE ~ med_incE + pct_renter + pct_ba + n_stations,
            data = model_df[!holdout, ], na.action = na.fail)
  oof[holdout] <- predict(fit, newdata = model_df[holdout, ])
}
stopifnot(all(is.finite(oof)))
sqrt(mean((model_df$med_rentE - oof)^2))


9. Choosing features without leaking information
Compare candidate feature sets on identical rows and folds. A variable with a small p-value need not improve prediction, and a useful predictor need not have a stable causal interpretation. Prefer an improvement that is repeatable and large enough to matter, rather than overinterpreting a tiny RMSE difference.
Imputation medians, scaling parameters, data-driven cutoffs, and feature selection must be learned from the training portion of each split. Otherwise information from validation observations leaks into model construction. Reusing CV scores to choose among many models also makes the winner’s reported score optimistic; an untouched final test set or nested CV provides a more independent assessment.
Randomly split neighboring tracts may be very similar. If deployment means predicting new neighborhoods or another city, geographically blocked validation can be more informative than random folds. Choose the split to match the intended prediction task.


10. Multicollinearity and heteroskedasticity
Multicollinearity means that predictors carry overlapping information. It can inflate coefficient standard errors, make coefficients unstable, and make individual effects hard to separate. Predictions within a similar predictor distribution may still be accurate. Perfect collinearity makes some coefficients unidentifiable; distribution changes and extrapolation can expose instability. Therefore “mostly harmless for prediction” is a qualified observation, not a rule.
Homoskedasticity is constant conditional error variance. A fan-shaped residual plot suggests heteroskedasticity: the uncertainty differs across observations. OLS slopes can remain unbiased under the zero-conditional-mean assumption, but conventional standard errors and prediction intervals can be wrong. Robust SEs address coefficient uncertainty under appropriate conditions; they do not repair a missing nonlinear relationship or automatically improve point predictions.
plot(fitted(m1), residuals(m1),
     xlab = "Fitted rent", ylab = "Residual")
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
# If installed: lmtest::bptest(m1)


11. Reading a residual map
Attach predictions and errors to the same tract rows, then use a diverging color scale centered on zero. A cluster of positive errors can suggest an omitted location-related feature, a nonlinear pattern, or correlated data problems. It does not identify a causal explanation by itself.
tracts$residual <- residuals(m1)  # only if no rows were silently omitted
ggplot(tracts) +
  geom_sf(aes(fill = residual), color = NA) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "white", high = "#b2182b",
                       midpoint = 0) +
  labs(fill = "Observed - fitted rent ($)") +
  theme_void()
Distinguish in-sample residual maps used for diagnosis from out-of-fold error maps used to inspect predictive performance. For policy triage, consider error size, survey MOE/CV, and whether the model was evaluated honestly.

title: Week 6: Feature Engineering and Fixed Effects
text:
Key Concepts

Feature engineering changes the information or functional form presented to a model. It should follow the question and be checked on held-out observations.
Logs express multiplicative changes; quadratic terms let a slope vary with a predictor; categories represent distinct groups.
Without interactions, category indicators shift intercepts. Interactions can make slopes differ across groups.
District fixed effects add district-specific intercepts. They do not explain which neighborhood mechanism causes a rent difference.
Compare models on the same rows, folds, and outcome scale. A log-scale RMSE and a dollar-scale RMSE cannot be ranked against each other.

title: Week 6: Feature Engineering and Fixed Effects
text:
Notes

1. Construct the analysis table carefully
The lecture uses 2023 ACS five-year estimates and reports 377 eligible tracts. That row count is a lecture result, not a promise about a fresh API download.








Feature
Construction
Meaning / caution




rent
rentE, ACS B25064_001
Median gross monthly rent; outcome in dollars


income
incomeE, B19013_001
Median annual household income in dollars


bldg_age
2023 - yr_builtE, B25035_001
Approximate age from median year built, not each building’s age


pct_renter
100 * hh_renterE / hh_totalE
Percentage of occupied units that are renter occupied


dist_ch_mi
Shortest tract-polygon distance to City Hall / 5280
Miles after projection to EPSG:2272

Tract polygon
Needed for distances, joins, and maps



library(tidycensus)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

tracts <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract", state = "PA", county = "Philadelphia",
  variables = c(rent = "B25064_001", income = "B19013_001",
                yr_built = "B25035_001", hh_total = "B25003_001",
                hh_renter = "B25003_003"),
  year = 2023, survey = "acs5", output = "wide", geometry = TRUE
) |> st_transform(2272)

city_hall <- st_sfc(st_point(c(-75.1636, 39.9526)), crs = 4326) |>
  st_transform(st_crs(tracts))

tracts <- tracts |>
  mutate(
    rent = rentE,
    income = incomeE,
    bldg_age = 2023 - yr_builtE,
    pct_renter = 100 * hh_renterE / hh_totalE,
    dist_ch_mi = as.numeric(st_distance(geometry, city_hall)) / 5280
  )

# Define eligibility once, before comparing models that need positive logs.
tracts <- tracts |>
  filter(is.finite(rent), rent > 0,
         is.finite(income), income > 0,
         is.finite(bldg_age), bldg_age >= 0,
         hh_totalE > 0, is.finite(pct_renter),
         between(pct_renter, 0, 100), is.finite(dist_ch_mi))
d <- st_drop_geometry(tracts)
EPSG:2272 uses US survey feet; it is not a meter CRS. The lecture’s division by 5280 follows its feet-to-miles convention. A tract containing City Hall has polygon-to-point distance zero. This feature is not centroid distance, walking distance, or the distance of every resident. Changing the distance definition changes the feature and potentially the answer.
Keep a record of excluded rows. ACS sampling uncertainty still exists after feature engineering; a transformed variable is not a more precise survey estimate.


2. Start with a baseline and a fixed evaluation design
The baseline is
f0 <- rent ~ income + pct_renter + bldg_age + dist_ch_mi
m0 <- lm(f0, data = d, na.action = na.fail)
The lecture assigns ten folds once. Every model must use that same assignment, not a freshly randomized split that may make a model look better by chance. This helper makes the fold assignment explicit instead of depending on a global variable. It computes pooled out-of-fold RMSE, not an unweighted average of ten separate RMSEs.
set.seed(5080)
fold_id <- sample(rep(1:10, length.out = nrow(d)))

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data, fold_id, log_outcome = FALSE) {
  stopifnot(length(fold_id) == nrow(data), !anyNA(fold_id))
  pred <- rep(NA_real_, nrow(data))
  for (k in sort(unique(fold_id))) {
    train <- fold_id != k
    fit <- lm(formula, data = data[train, , drop = FALSE],
              na.action = na.fail)
    p <- predict(fit, newdata = data[!train, , drop = FALSE])
    if (log_outcome) p <- exp(p)  # the lecture's back-transformation rule
    pred[!train] <- p
  }
  stopifnot(all(is.finite(pred)), all(is.finite(data$rent)))
  sqrt(mean((data$rent - pred)^2))
}

cv_rmse(f0, d, fold_id)
All imputation, learned scaling, data-driven cutoffs, feature selection, and optional log-bias correction must be fitted using each training fold only. Fixed, pre-specified rules such as log(income) and a two-mile boundary do not estimate parameters from the held-out outcomes. The final test set remains untouched during model selection.


3. Log-transform a predictor: diminishing marginal dollar changes
f1 <- rent ~ log(income) + pct_renter + bldg_age + dist_ch_mi
R’s log() is the natural logarithm. Equal ratios have equal log differences: doubling 20,000 to 40,000 and doubling 40,000 to 80,000 both change log income by \(\log(2)\). This lets a model represent a relationship where another dollar of income matters less at higher income levels.
For \(Y=\beta_0+\beta_1\log(X)+\cdots\), multiplying \(X\) by \(r\) changes the fitted level of \(Y\) by \(\beta_1\log(r)\), holding the other predictors fixed. The lecture coefficient is about 502.1787: a 1% income increase corresponds to approximately 5.02 dollars more monthly rent, or exactly \(502.1787\log(1.01)\approx5.00\) dollars. It does not mean 502 dollars per additional dollar of income.



Log-income and quadratic-age relationships. These are illustrations, not fitted Philadelphia observations.


A skewed predictor does not itself violate an OLS requirement: OLS does not require the predictors to be normally distributed. Use logs because the relationship or variance structure suggests them, then examine fit and validation.
Zeros and missing values: log(0) is -Inf; negative values do not have a real natural log. log1p(x) computes log(1 + x) and can be useful for nonnegative counts containing zero. It is not a universally interchangeable substitute for log(x): its percentage interpretation differs near zero and depends on the measurement units. Investigate negative sentinel values rather than adding an arbitrary constant to everything.


4. Log-transform the outcome: interpret changes in percentages
f2 <- log(rent) ~ log(income) + pct_renter + bldg_age + dist_ch_mi
The four common forms have different interpretations. These describe the fitted relationship with all other included variables held fixed.







Model component
Interpretation of coefficient \(\beta\)




\(Y\sim X\)
One extra X unit corresponds to \(\beta\) Y units


\(Y\sim\log(X)\)
1% more X corresponds to approximately \(\beta/100\) Y units; exact \(\beta\log(1.01)\)


\(\log(Y)\sim X\)
One extra X unit changes the back-transformed fitted value by approximately \(100\beta\)%; exact \(100(e^\beta-1)\)%


\(\log(Y)\sim\log(X)\)
1% more X changes the back-transformed fitted value by approximately \(\beta\)%; exact \(100(1.01^\beta-1)\)%



The lecture’s log-income coefficient is 0.3633423. It is an elasticity: a 1% income increase is associated with roughly a 0.363% increase in the back-transformed fitted rent. A 10% increase is about \(100(1.10^{0.3633423}-1)\approx3.52\)%, not 36.3%.
For pct_renter, a one-unit increase means one percentage point because the feature is coded 0–100. Do not confuse a percentage point in X with a percentage change in Y.

Compare predictions in dollars
log_fit <- lm(f2, data = d, na.action = na.fail)
rent_pred <- exp(predict(log_fit, newdata = d))
cv_rmse(f2, d, fold_id, log_outcome = TRUE)
The HTML reports an in-sample log RMSE of about 0.1885 and a back-transformed dollar RMSE of about 259.55. They use different units; 0.1885 is not evidence that the model beats a 265-dollar held-out RMSE. Both the scale and the evaluation sample have changed in that comparison.
There is a further subtlety: exp(predicted_log_rent) estimates the exponential of the conditional mean of log rent, not generally the arithmetic conditional mean of rent. It corresponds to a conditional median under a symmetric log-error distribution. Because exponentiation is nonlinear, simple exponentiation can underpredict the mean. A smearing correction can multiply by the mean of exp(residuals(fit)), under suitable error-distribution assumptions. If used in CV, estimate that correction from training residuals only. The reported lecture comparison uses simple exponentiation; do not silently change that rule and label the resulting score as the same experiment.



5. Add a squared term: curvature without changing model family
The next lecture model returns to rent in dollars; the models are not all cumulative additions to the log-outcome model.
f3 <- rent ~ log(income) + pct_renter + bldg_age +
  I(bldg_age^2) + dist_ch_mi
I() means “interpret this arithmetic as written.” In an R formula, ^ otherwise has a special formula meaning. Include the linear age term as well as its square. The model is curved in age but still linear in its coefficients, so it is still a linear regression.
The lecture age coefficients are approximately \(\beta_1=-28.00445\) and \(\beta_2=0.1823244\):
\[
\frac{\partial\widehat{rent}}{\partial age}
=\beta_1+2\beta_2 age,
\qquad age^*=-\frac{\beta_1}{2\beta_2}\approx76.8.
\]
The marginal slope is therefore not a constant −28 dollars per year. It becomes less negative as age increases and is positive beyond the fitted turning point. The source reports ages roughly 5–85, so little data lie beyond that turn. Check the original ACS coding and oldest-year category before interpreting a pile-up of very old housing. A curve near the edge of the data is not proof that aging a particular building raises its rent. Extrapolating a quadratic far outside the observed ages is especially risky.


6. Categories and reference groups
The lecture replaces continuous City Hall distance with three rings:
d <- d |>
  mutate(
    ring = case_when(
      is.na(dist_ch_mi) ~ NA_character_,
      dist_ch_mi < 2 ~ "Core",
      dist_ch_mi < 5 ~ "Inner",
      TRUE ~ "Outer"
    ),
    ring = factor(ring, levels = c("Core", "Inner", "Outer")),
    renter_band = cut(pct_renter, breaks = c(0, 33, 66, 100),
                      labels = c("Low", "Medium", "High"),
                      include.lowest = TRUE)
  )
f4 <- rent ~ log(income) + pct_renter + bldg_age + I(bldg_age^2) + ring
The ring boundaries are [0, 2), [2, 5), and [5, infinity): exactly two miles is Inner and exactly five is Outer. For the cut() example, the default is right-closed, so the intervals are [0,33], (33,66], and (66,100]. Writing an explicit missing-value branch prevents unknown distance from being silently classified as Outer.
With an intercept and the usual treatment contrasts, a factor with \(k\) levels has \(k-1\) indicator coefficients. Core is the reference here. The lecture’s Inner coefficient of −122.28 and Outer coefficient of −164.19 represent dollar differences from Core at the same values of the other predictors.
d$ring <- relevel(d$ring, ref = "Outer")
# Refit the same formula on the same rows to change the comparison group.
# Restore Core before interpreting the lecture interaction coefficients below.
d$ring <- relevel(d$ring, ref = "Core")
Changing only the reference group changes coefficient labels and the intercept, not fitted predictions or RMSE. With Outer as reference, the same example gives Core +164.19 and Inner about +41.92. A no-intercept specification can instead use one indicator for every category.
Categories simplify interpretation but discard within-bin differences: 2.1 and 4.9 miles now receive the same ring contribution. Choose meaningful boundaries; do not expect binning automatically to improve prediction.


7. Interactions: an effect can depend on another variable
f5 <- rent ~ log(income) * ring + pct_renter + bldg_age + I(bldg_age^2)
# log(income) * ring expands to:
# log(income) + ring + log(income):ring
With Core as reference, the income slope in Inner is the main log-income coefficient plus the Inner interaction coefficient. The interaction coefficient alone is the difference in slopes, not the full Inner slope.








Ring
Lecture log-income slope
Approximate dollars for 1% more income




Core
653.6974
6.54


Inner
653.6974 − 219.1028 = 434.5946
4.35


Outer
653.6974 − 244.4214 = 409.2760
4.09



Once an interaction is present, a ring’s main coefficient is its difference from Core at log(income) = 0, meaning income equals one dollar—not the usual tract. The group difference at a meaningful income also includes the interaction term. Centering log income around a meaningful reference makes that intercept comparison easier to understand; any sample-estimated centering constant belongs inside the training-fold workflow.



Category shifts, interactions, and fixed effects. All line positions are illustrative.




8. Planning-district fixed effects
Fixed effects here mean one intercept adjustment per planning district, not a new causal estimation technique by itself. A simplified model is
\[
rent_i=\alpha_{district(i)}+\beta\log(income_i)+\gamma'Z_i+\epsilon_i.
\]
There are 18 districts in the lecture. Under ordinary treatment coding with an intercept, this yields 17 district indicators. Treat a district ID as a factor, not a continuous number.
# districts: planning-district polygons loaded from the city's spatial data
districts <- st_transform(districts, st_crs(tracts))
tracts_fe <- st_join(
  tracts,
  districts |> select(district = dist_name),
  largest = TRUE
) |>
  mutate(district = factor(district))

# Check validity, missing districts, one row per original GEOID, and counts.
stopifnot(nrow(tracts_fe) == nrow(tracts),
          !anyDuplicated(tracts_fe$GEOID))
d_fe <- st_drop_geometry(tracts_fe)
table(d_fe$district, useNA = "ifany")
f6 <- rent ~ log(income) + pct_renter + bldg_age + I(bldg_age^2) + district
largest = TRUE assigns the district with the largest overlap for each tract. This is an area-overlap rule, not a centroid rule. Check invalid polygons, unmatched tracts, and ambiguous ties. Tract boundaries can cross districts; one district per tract is a modeling simplification.
The lecture’s log-income coefficient drops from roughly 519.74 to 427.39 after including district effects. The coefficient now reflects comparisons within districts, conditional on the other predictors. District indicators absorb additive differences common to each district. They do not eliminate confounding that varies within districts, identify specific amenities, or prove causality.
An in-sample residual map can become less clustered because the model has more location parameters. That is a useful diagnostic, not independent evidence of better prediction. Use the same diverging color limits for before/after maps and check held-out errors as well.

Rare districts and unseen factor levels
One source district has only one tract. If that tract is held out, there is no training observation from which to estimate its district effect. predict.lm() can fail on a new factor level; merely defining factor labels does not supply an estimable coefficient.
The lecture’s CV variant merges very small districts into a coarser grouping called district_cv. Thus its reported CV score uses merged groups, whereas some preceding coefficient and residual illustrations use the original districts. Keep this distinction in the experiment log.
Before CV, inspect how many training examples of each category remain in every fold. A group size threshold such as ten does not mathematically guarantee coverage in every random split. Use a documented, geographically sensible coarser geography and an explicit missing/unseen-category policy. Nearest-polygon distance can tie at zero for neighbors, so an automatic nearest-feature merge is not necessarily a meaningful district assignment.
District fixed effects can predict new tracts in represented districts. They do not automatically predict a wholly unseen district. Grouped or spatially blocked validation tests a harder deployment question than a random tract split.



9. Compare the experiments, not just the formulas
These are the rounded ten-fold pooled RMSE values printed in the supplied lecture, in dollars per month. They have not been rerun against the live ACS.

Return to dollar rent; add quadratic age to m1

Replace distance with rings in m3

Model comparison using values transcribed from the lecture, not fresh estimates.


The district model performs best in this particular log. Its improvement from 265 to 256 is about nine dollars, or 3.4%. Small differences should be checked for stability across repeated splits and, after selection, an untouched test sample. More complicated terms do not necessarily reduce held-out error.
A useful experiment log records the formula, outcome scale, eligible rows, fold IDs, preprocessing, back-transformation rule, category handling, and metric. Do not compare the Week 5 average-fold score directly with a Week 6 pooled score and attribute every difference to feature engineering.

Check Your Understanding

In rent ~ log(income), the log-income coefficient is 500. Is a 1% income increase associated with about 5 dollars or 500 dollars more rent?
In log(rent) ~ log(income), what does an income coefficient of 0.36 mean?
Can a log-scale RMSE of 0.19 be directly compared with a dollar RMSE of 265?
Why write I(bldg_age^2) rather than interpreting the age coefficient alone?
With Core as the reference, the income slope is 650 and the Inner interaction coefficient is −220. What is Inner’s full slope?
Does changing the reference from Core to Outer change predictions?
Why can a one-tract district cause cross-validation to fail?
Does a lower RMSE after adding district effects prove a district causes rent to rise? Does it identify which amenity matters?

Answers: 1. About 5 dollars; exact change is 500 * log(1.01). 2. About 0.36% higher fitted rent for 1% more income, conditional on other terms. 3. No: transform predictions and use the same outcome scale and evaluation rows. 4. The quadratic gives a changing slope; I() requests arithmetic squaring. 5. 430. 6. No, if only the reference coding changes on the same sample. 7. Its category can be absent from a training fold, so its intercept cannot be estimated. 8. No to both: predictive improvement is not causal identification.

Reflection
Feature engineering is a way to express plausible relationships, not a checklist of tricks that must improve a model. My biggest distinction is between a group intercept and a group-specific slope, and between better fit to existing places and successful prediction in places the model has not seen.
