title: Week 3: Visualization, Geoms, and ggplot2
text:
We used data visualization to reveal patterns that summary statistics can hide. The class introduced Anscombe’s quartet, the Grammar of Graphics, the structure of a ggplot2 plot, common geoms, and ways to represent uncertainty in American Community Survey (ACS) estimates.
We also connected visualization to data quality by calculating coefficients of variation, propagating margins of error for derived estimates, and testing whether change over time is statistically distinguishable from sampling error.

title: Week 3: Visualization, Geoms, and ggplot2
text:
We used data visualization to reveal patterns that summary statistics can hide. The class introduced Anscombe’s quartet, the Grammar of Graphics, the structure of a ggplot2 plot, common geoms, and ways to represent uncertainty in American Community Survey (ACS) estimates.
We also connected visualization to data quality by calculating coefficients of variation, propagating margins of error for derived estimates, and testing whether change over time is statistically distinguishable from sampling error.

title: Week 3: Visualization, Geoms, and ggplot2
text:
Key Concepts

A graph is a mapping from variables in a dataset to visual properties such as position, color, size, shape, and transparency.
Anscombe’s quartet shows why summary statistics alone are not enough: very different datasets can share nearly identical means, variances, correlations, and regression lines.
In ggplot2, data and aesthetic mappings are combined with one or more geom layers.
Put a variable inside aes() when it should control a visual property; put a constant outside aes() when it is only decoration.
Choose a geom based on the analytical question and the types of variables involved.
ACS margins of error describe sampling uncertainty and should be shown or evaluated alongside estimates.
For ACS data published after 2005, a 90% margin of error equals 1.645 standard errors.

title: Week 3: Visualization, Geoms, and ggplot2
text:
1. Why Visualization Matters: Anscombe’s Quartet



Anscombe’s quartet


Anscombe’s quartet contains four datasets with nearly identical numerical summaries, including the mean of x, mean of y, variance of x, variance of y, correlation, and fitted linear regression equation. However, the scatterplots reveal four very different structures: an approximately linear relationship, a curved relationship, an influential outlier, and a vertical cluster with one high-leverage point.
The lesson is not that statistics are unhelpful. The lesson is that numerical summaries and visualizations should be used together. A model can appear reasonable in a table while being misleading when the underlying pattern is plotted.

title: Week 3: Visualization, Geoms, and ggplot2
text:
2. The Grammar of Graphics
The Grammar of Graphics treats a plot as a combination of components:

Data: the table being visualized.
Aesthetic mappings: how variables map to x-position, y-position, color, fill, size, shape, or alpha.
Geoms: the marks drawn on the page, such as points, lines, bars, boxes, or intervals.
Scales: how data values are translated into positions, colors, sizes, and labels.
Facets: small multiples that divide the data into panels.
Coordinates: the coordinate system and axis orientation.
Theme: non-data styling such as fonts, grid lines, and background.

A minimal plot follows this pattern:
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(data = tract_data, aes(x = population, y = moe_pct)) +
  geom_point()

ggplot() initializes the plot and supplies the default data.
aes() defines the default mappings from data columns to visual properties.
geom_point() adds a layer that draws one point for each observation.
The + operator adds layers and other components to the plot.

R is case-sensitive, so the correct function is geom_point(), not geom_Point().

title: Week 3: Visualization, Geoms, and ggplot2
text:
3. Mapping Variables vs. Setting Constants
A variable placed inside aes() is mapped to a visual property:
ggplot(tract_data, aes(x = population, y = moe_pct)) +
  geom_point(aes(color = reliability))
Here, each value of reliability receives a color, and ggplot2 creates a legend.
A value placed outside aes() is set as a constant:
ggplot(tract_data, aes(x = population, y = moe_pct)) +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 2, alpha = 0.7)
Here, every point is steel blue, size 2, and slightly transparent. These choices decorate the layer and do not represent additional variables.
A common mistake is aes(color = “blue”). Because “blue” is inside aes(), ggplot2 treats it as a category label rather than as a literal color. Use color = “blue” outside aes() to make all points blue.

title: Week 3: Visualization, Geoms, and ggplot2
section: 4. Choosing a Geom from the Question
text:
4. Choosing a Geom from the Question








Analytical question
Typical geom
Notes




How is one continuous variable distributed?
geom_histogram() or geom_density()
A histogram groups values into bins; bin width changes the visual story.


How do two continuous variables relate?
geom_point()
Add geom_smooth() only when a fitted trend is useful and appropriate.


How does a continuous variable differ across groups?
geom_boxplot() or geom_violin()
A boxplot summarizes the distribution; raw points can reveal sample size and outliers.


How many observations fall in each category?
geom_bar()
geom_bar() counts rows automatically.


What value has already been calculated for each category?
geom_col()
The bar height comes from a y variable in the data.


How does a value change over ordered time?
geom_line() plus geom_point()
Set the group aesthetic when multiple series are present.


How uncertain is an estimate?
geom_errorbar(), geom_linerange(), geom_pointrange(), or geom_ribbon()
Map lower and upper bounds explicitly.



The misspelling geom_poxplot() in the original notes should be geom_boxplot().

title: Week 3: Visualization, Geoms, and ggplot2
section: 5. Showing ACS Estimates with Margins of Error
text:
5. Showing ACS Estimates with Margins of Error
ACS tables usually provide an estimate and a margin of error at the 90% confidence level. A simple interval plot makes both visible:
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

tract_data |>
  mutate(
    lower = estimate - moe,
    upper = estimate + moe
  ) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = reorder(NAME, estimate), y = estimate)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower, ymax = upper), width = 0.2) +
  coord_flip() +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Estimate with 90% MOE")
A large interval is not automatically a reason to discard an observation. It means the estimate is less precise and should be interpreted, compared, or mapped cautiously.

title: Week 3: Visualization, Geoms, and ggplot2
text:
6. Coefficient of Variation and Reliability
The coefficient of variation (CV) expresses sampling error relative to the size of the estimate. Because the published ACS MOE is based on a 90% confidence level:
SE = MOE / 1.645
CV = (SE / estimate) × 100
   = (MOE / (1.645 × estimate)) × 100
In R:
tract_data <- tract_data |>
  mutate(
    se = moe / 1.645,
    cv = abs(se / estimate) * 100,
    reliability = case_when(
      cv <= 15 ~ "high",
      cv <= 30 ~ "medium",
      TRUE ~ "low"
    )
  )
A common classroom interpretation is:

CV at or below 15%: high reliability.
CV above 15% and at or below 30%: medium reliability.
CV above 30%: low reliability and high relative sampling error.

These cutoffs are practical categories, not universal laws. CV is also unstable or undefined when an estimate is zero or very close to zero, and it can be hard to interpret for estimates that may be negative. In those cases, inspect the estimate and MOE directly.

title: Week 3: Visualization, Geoms, and ggplot2
section: 7. Margins of Error for Derived Estimates
text:
7. Margins of Error for Derived Estimates
When estimates are combined, their margins of error cannot usually be added or divided directly. Uncertainty must be propagated with an appropriate formula.
The tidycensus package provides helper functions:

moe_sum(): the MOE for a sum of several estimates.
moe_prop(): the MOE for a proportion when the numerator is a subset of the denominator, such as people below poverty divided by the population for whom poverty status is determined.
moe_ratio(): the MOE for a ratio when the numerator is not a subset of the denominator.
moe_product(): the MOE for a product of two estimates.

The estimate itself and its derived MOE are separate outputs. Check the documentation and supply both estimate and MOE inputs in the order required by the selected function.

title: Week 3: Visualization, Geoms, and ggplot2
text:
8. Comparing Change over Time
ACS 5-year estimates describe a five-year period, not a single point in time. Avoid comparing overlapping periods such as 2018–2022 and 2019–2023 because four years of underlying data are shared. For a cleaner comparison, use non-overlapping periods such as 2014–2018 and 2019–2023.
Suppose the estimates and published 90% MOEs are:

2014–2018: $45,000 ± $8,000
2019–2023: $62,000 ± $11,000

First convert each MOE to a standard error:
SE1 = 8,000 / 1.645 = 4,863
SE2 = 11,000 / 1.645 = 6,687
For two non-overlapping estimates, the approximate standard error of the difference is:
Difference = 62,000 - 45,000 = 17,000
SEdiff = sqrt(SE1² + SE2²)
       = sqrt(4,863² + 6,687²)
       ≈ 8,269
The z statistic is:
z = Difference / SEdiff
  = 17,000 / 8,269
  ≈ 2.06
At the ACS standard 90% confidence level, compare the absolute z value with 1.645. Because 2.06 > 1.645, the estimated increase is statistically significant at the 90% level.
The 90% MOE and confidence interval for the change are:
MOE of difference = 1.645 × 8,269 ≈ 13,600
90% interval       = 17,000 ± 13,600
                   ≈ [$3,400, $30,600]
The original calculation ended with $1,369; the correct value is approximately $13,600. Statistical significance does not automatically imply that the change is large enough to matter for policy, and the calculation addresses sampling error rather than every possible source of bias.

title: Week 3: Visualization, Geoms, and ggplot2
text:
Reflection
This week showed me why data visualization is part of analysis rather than a final decoration step. Anscombe’s quartet demonstrates that identical summary statistics can hide very different data structures. The Grammar of Graphics gives me a systematic way to build a plot by connecting variables, aesthetics, and geoms. For ACS data, I also need to visualize and calculate uncertainty so that a precise-looking estimate is not mistaken for a certain one.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Joins, CRS, and sf
text:
We connected ordinary Census tables to map geometries, compared attribute joins with spatial joins, and learned how the sf package stores spatial features in R. We then studied coordinate reference systems (CRSs), datums, projections, EPSG codes, UTM and State Plane systems, and the distortion tradeoffs involved in flattening the Earth onto a map.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Joins, CRS, and sf
text:
Key Concepts

A GEOID is a Census geography identifier. Store it as character text so leading zeros are not lost.
An attribute join matches rows using a shared key such as GEOID; a spatial join matches features using their locations and shapes.
An sf object is a data-frame-like table with a special geometry column and CRS metadata.
A CRS explains what coordinate numbers mean and where they locate features on Earth.
st_set_crs() assigns or repairs a CRS label; st_transform() actually recalculates coordinates in another CRS.
Geographic CRSs normally use longitude and latitude in degrees. Projected CRSs use flat x/y coordinates, commonly in meters or feet.
Every flat projection distorts something. Choose a projection according to the task: shape, area, distance, or direction.
Spatial predicates answer yes/no relationship questions. Spatial transformations such as buffers, intersections, and unions create new geometry.

    B[2015 table<br/>100, 200, 400] --> J

    J --> I[inner_join<br/>100, 200]
    J --> F[full_join<br/>100, 200, 300, 400]







left_join()
income_joined <- left_join(income_23, income_15, by = "GEOID")

GEOID 400 does not appear in this result because it exists only in the right-hand table. The original note incorrectly included 400 in the left_join() result; including all four GEOIDs would be a full_join().


Join types







Join
Rows retained




left_join(x, y)
All keys from x; unmatched y values become NA


inner_join(x, y)
Only keys appearing in both x and y


full_join(x, y)
Every key appearing in either table


anti_join(x, y)
Rows in x with no match in y; useful for diagnosing failed matches



Always check a join rather than assuming it worked:
income_joined |>
  summarize(
    rows = n(),
    missing_2015 = sum(is.na(med_inc_15))
  )

anti_join(income_23, income_15, by = "GEOID")
Matching GEOIDs alone may still be misleading across years if Census boundaries changed. For time comparisons, confirm that the geographic vintage is consistent or use an appropriate crosswalk.

section: 2. sf: Attributes and Geometry in One Table
text:
2. sf: Attributes and Geometry in One Table
sf means simple features. An sf object behaves like a data frame but also contains:

Ordinary attribute columns such as GEOID, population, or income.
A geometry column containing POINT, LINESTRING, POLYGON, or multipart geometries.
CRS metadata describing the coordinate system.




GEOID
med_inc_23
geometry




42101000100
82,000
POLYGON (…)


42101000200
31,500
POLYGON (…)



The geometry column is often described as sticky: when an sf object is the left table in a normal dplyr operation, its geometry usually remains attached.
library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(tidycensus)

tracts <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = c(median_income = "B19013_001"),
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  geometry = TRUE
)

class(tracts)
st_geometry_type(tracts)
st_crs(tracts)
For an attribute join, normally join a plain table onto the sf layer:
tracts_with_data <- left_join(tracts, income_table, by = "GEOID")
If both inputs are sf objects but the match is based on a key rather than location, drop geometry from the right table first:
joined <- left_join(spatial_x, st_drop_geometry(spatial_y), by = "GEOID")

Common spatial formats

A shapefile is not only one .shp file. It normally includes .shp geometry, .shx index, .dbf attributes, and .prj CRS information. Keep the companion files together.
A file geodatabase has a .gdb extension and is usually a folder containing multiple layers.
GeoPackage (.gpkg) is a modern single-file container that can hold several vector layers.
st_read() or read_sf() reads supported vector layers into sf.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Joins, CRS, and sf
text:
3. What a CRS Does
A CRS answers four questions:

What model of Earth is being used?
Where is that model anchored relative to Earth?
How are locations represented as coordinates?
What units and axis conventions do those coordinates use?






flowchart LR
    E[Real Earth] --> D[Datum and ellipsoid<br/>model and anchor]
    D --> G[Geographic CRS<br/>longitude and latitude]
    G --> P[Map projection]
    P --> C[Projected CRS<br/>x and y in linear units]







Geographic CRS

Represents longitude and latitude on an ellipsoid.
Coordinate values are angular, normally degrees.
Useful for data exchange, GPS, and global reference.
A degree is not a fixed ground distance: one degree of longitude becomes shorter toward the poles.



Projected CRS

Converts locations to a flat x/y grid.
Units are usually meters or feet.
Designed for a particular region and purpose.
Often preferable for local buffers, Euclidean distances, and areas because the units are explicit and distortion can be controlled locally.

Modern sf can perform geodesic calculations on longitude/latitude data, but for a local policy analysis it is still important to choose and document an appropriate projected CRS before interpreting feet, meters, areas, or buffer radii.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Joins, CRS, and sf
text:
4. Ellipsoids and Datums
An ellipsoid approximates Earth’s shape. A datum connects that model to the real Earth and supplies a reference frame. GRS 80 is an ellipsoid; NAD 83 is a datum/reference system built on it.







Reference
Main idea




NAD 27
North American Datum of 1927; based on the Clarke 1866 ellipsoid and anchored at Meades Ranch, Kansas


NAD 83
North American Datum of 1983; based on GRS 80 and designed as an Earth-centered reference system


WGS 84
Global Earth-centered reference system used by GPS and much worldwide data



Coordinates for the same physical place can differ between datums. A CRS label is therefore essential; longitude and latitude numbers without a datum are incomplete information.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Joins, CRS, and sf
section: 5. Flattening Earth: Projection Families and Distortion
text:
5. Flattening Earth: Projection Families and Distortion
A globe cannot be flattened without stretching, tearing, or compressing it. A map projection chooses where and how distortion occurs.





flowchart TD
    E[Curved Earth] --> CY[Cylindrical]
    E --> CO[Conic]
    E --> AZ[Planar or azimuthal]
    CY --> TM[Transverse Mercator<br/>used by UTM]
    CO --> LCC[Lambert conformal conic<br/>common in State Plane]
    CO --> AEA[Albers equal area<br/>regional area analysis]
    AZ --> LOCAL[Directions or distances<br/>from a selected center]







Cylindrical: imagine wrapping a cylinder around Earth. A transverse cylinder is turned sideways so its line of best fit follows a meridian.
Conic: imagine placing a cone over Earth. It works well for mid-latitude regions that extend east–west.
Planar or azimuthal: project onto a plane touching at a point; often useful around a chosen center.
Tangent projections touch at one line or point; secant projections cut through and create two standard lines. Distortion is lowest along the standard line(s) or point and generally increases away from them.


What can a projection preserve?








Property
What it preserves
What it does not guarantee




Conformal
Local angles and small shapes
Correct area or distance everywhere


Equal-area
Relative area
Local shape and all distances


Equidistant
Selected distances from particular lines or points
Every distance between every pair of locations


True-direction / azimuthal
Directions from a selected center
Shape, area, and distance everywhere



No flat map preserves shape, area, distance, and direction everywhere at the same time. The correct projection depends on the research question.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Joins, CRS, and sf
text:
7. st_set_crs() Is Not st_transform()
This distinction is essential:





flowchart LR
    A[Coordinates have no label<br/>but true CRS is known] -->|st_set_crs 2272| B[Same coordinate numbers<br/>correct CRS metadata added]
    B -->|st_transform 4326| C[New coordinate numbers<br/>same real-world locations]







st_set_crs()
Use only when coordinates already belong to a known CRS but the CRS metadata is missing or incorrect.
roads <- st_set_crs(roads, 2272)
This changes the label, not the coordinate numbers and not the locations. Assigning the wrong label makes the data incorrect.


st_transform()
Use when the layer already has the correct source CRS and you want a new CRS.
roads_wgs84 <- st_transform(roads, 4326)
This recalculates all coordinate numbers while preserving the same real-world locations. Before combining spatial layers, make their CRSs compatible:
st_crs(stations) == st_crs(tracts)
stations <- st_transform(stations, st_crs(tracts))

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Joins, CRS, and sf
text:
8. UTM and State Plane Systems

UTM
The Universal Transverse Mercator system divides the world into 60 longitudinal zones, each approximately 6 degrees wide. Each zone uses its own transverse Mercator projection and meter coordinates.





flowchart LR
    W[World longitude] --> Z1[Zone 1<br/>6 degrees]
    W --> Z2[Zone 2<br/>6 degrees]
    W --> DOT[...]
    W --> Z18[Zone 18N<br/>Philadelphia region]
    W --> Z60[Zone 60<br/>6 degrees]






A central meridian runs through each zone. UTM assigns a false easting of 500,000 meters at that meridian so ordinary zone coordinates avoid negative eastings. Southern-hemisphere zones also use a false northing. A coordinate such as x = 500,000 and y = 4,400,000 has meaning only together with its UTM zone and hemisphere.


State Plane
The State Plane Coordinate System divides US states into one or more zones designed for accurate local work. Pennsylvania has North and South zones. EPSG:2272 is the NAD83 Pennsylvania South definition in US survey feet. Do not assume that every State Plane layer uses feet: definitions may use meters or feet, so inspect the exact EPSG record.

text:
9. Spatial Predicates: What Relationship Do the Shapes Have?
Imagine polygon A next to B, while smaller polygon C lies inside A:





flowchart LR
    A[Polygon A] ---|touches boundary| B[Polygon B]
    C[Polygon C] -->|within| A
    A -->|contains| C

















Predicate
Question
A–B
A–C
C–A
A–A




st_intersects()
Do the features share any point?
TRUE
TRUE
TRUE
TRUE


st_touches()
Do boundaries meet while interiors do not overlap?
TRUE
FALSE
FALSE
FALSE


st_within()
Is the first feature inside the second?
FALSE
FALSE
TRUE
TRUE



Important details:

st_intersects() is broad: touching, overlapping, containment, and equality can all count as intersection.
st_touches() is usually better for finding neighboring polygons because a feature does not touch itself.
st_within(x, y) has an order: it asks whether x is within y.
Spatial predicates normally return sparse relationship lists or logical relationships; they do not automatically create clipped shapes.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Joins, CRS, and sf
text:
10. Selecting, Joining, and Changing Geometry
These functions answer different questions:








Function
Main result
Does geometry change?




st_filter(x, y)
Rows of x satisfying a spatial predicate with y
No; selected x geometries remain whole


st_join(x, y)
x features plus matching attributes from y
Normally keeps x geometry


st_intersection(x, y)
Shared pieces of x and y
Yes; features may be clipped or split


st_union(x)
Combined geometry
Yes; boundaries may dissolve


st_buffer(x, dist)
Zones at a specified distance around x
Yes; creates new polygons


st_distance(x, y)
Pairwise distance matrix
No








flowchart TD
    Q[Which tracts are near a station?] --> F[st_filter<br/>keep whole matching tracts]
    Q --> J[st_join<br/>attach station or tract attributes]
    Q --> X[st_intersection<br/>create only overlapping pieces]
    Q --> U[st_union<br/>merge all service zones]







Why st_filter() and st_intersection() are not interchangeable
If a half-mile station buffer touches only a corner of a tract:

st_filter(tracts, buffer) returns the complete tract.
st_intersection(tracts, buffer) returns only the portion inside the buffer.

Choose based on the research question. Counting every tract with any overlap is not the same as measuring how much tract area or population lies within the service zone.


Spatial joins
stations_with_tract <- st_join(
  stations,
  tracts,
  join = st_within
)
This keeps station geometry and adds attributes of the tract containing each station. If one x feature matches multiple y features, st_join() can produce multiple output rows, so check the row count.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Joins, CRS, and sf
text:
11. Half-Mile Station Access Example
Research question: How many Census tracts are near a transit station?





flowchart LR
    S[Stations] --> C[Transform to local projected CRS]
    T[Census tracts] --> C
    C --> B[Create half-mile station buffers]
    B --> F[Filter or intersect tracts]
    F --> N[Count, summarize, and map]






library(sf)
library(dplyr)
library(units)

# Both layers must use the same suitable projected CRS
stations_pa <- st_transform(stations, 2272)
tracts_pa <- st_transform(tracts, 2272)

half_mile <- set_units(0.5, mi)
station_buffers <- st_buffer(stations_pa, dist = half_mile)

# Criterion: any part of the tract intersects any buffer
near_tracts <- st_filter(
  tracts_pa,
  station_buffers,
  .predicate = st_intersects
)

nrow(near_tracts)
The result depends on the definition of near:

Any-overlap rule: a tract counts when any part intersects the buffer. This can count a large tract touched only at one corner.
Representative-point rule: test a centroid or st_point_on_surface() against the buffer. This is simpler but does not describe where residents actually live.
Area or population share rule: intersect the tract with the buffer and calculate the portion covered. This is more informative but requires stronger assumptions and more work.

To merge overlapping station buffers into one service area:
service_area <- st_union(station_buffers)

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Joins, CRS, and sf
text:
12. Distance Matrices and Nearest Features
d <- st_distance(stations_pa, tracts_pa)
st_distance(x, y) returns a matrix:

Rows correspond to features in x.
Columns correspond to features in y.
Cell [i, j] is the distance between x feature i and y feature j.
Units follow the CRS and sf calculation method.

For many features, the full matrix can be large. If the question is only nearest station, use st_nearest_feature() and then calculate paired distances:
tract_points <- st_point_on_surface(tracts_pa)
nearest_id <- st_nearest_feature(tract_points, stations_pa)

tracts_pa <- tracts_pa |>
  mutate(
    nearest_station = stations_pa$station_id[nearest_id],
    station_distance = st_distance(
      tract_points,
      stations_pa[nearest_id, ],
      by_element = TRUE
    )
  )

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Joins, CRS, and sf
text:
13. A Reliable Spatial-Analysis Checklist

Inspect both the attributes and geometry types.
Confirm GEOID type, geography level, vintage, uniqueness, and missing values.
Inspect each layer with st_crs().
Use st_set_crs() only when the correct missing label is known.
Use st_transform() to put layers in the CRS appropriate to the analysis.
Confirm the units before distances, areas, or buffers.
Choose the spatial predicate that matches the policy question.
Decide whether features should remain whole or be clipped.
Check output row counts, duplicated matches, NA values, empty geometries, and validity.
Map the result as a visual quality check.

title: Week 4: Spatial Data, Joins, CRS, and sf
text:
Reflection
This week helped me understand that a map is not separate from a data table. In sf, every row contains both attributes and a spatial feature, and either a shared key or a spatial relationship can connect datasets. I also learned that CRS choice is part of the analysis: assigning the wrong CRS label, measuring in unknown units, or choosing a projection that distorts the property I care about can make a technically successful workflow produce a wrong answer.
The most important distinction for me is between selecting features and changing geometry. st_filter() keeps complete features that meet a condition, whereas st_intersection() creates the actual shared pieces. Before asking R to count tracts near a station, I must first define what near means.

For transit access, should a tract count when any part touches a buffer, when its representative point is inside, or when a certain share of residents is covered?
